raw_evidence.label: Origin: The Economist's 2018 graphic-detail piece
raw_evidence.content: On 24 November 2018 The Economist published a Graphic Detail piece titled 'TV's golden age is real' (print headline: 'The end of channel surfing'). The piece argued that the contemporary belief in a 'golden age' of television was, against many cultural pundits' instinct, supported by hard data. To make that case the paper pulled raw text dumps from IMDb's public interfaces, joined them with OMDb (Open Movie Database) for region and air-date metadata, and produced a season-level dataset of 2,266 American TV-drama seasons spanning 1990 to 2018. Each row represents a single season (e.g. Breaking Bad season 5) carrying an IMDb-weighted average rating, a 'share' of votes received by that season relative to the show, the air date of the season's first episode, and a list of genres. The CSV used in this analysis is the actual artifact behind that scatter chart, published openly in The Economist's graphic-detail-data GitHub repository.

raw_evidence.label: Dataset shape and coverage
raw_evidence.content: The dataset covers 2,266 seasons of 868 distinct TV dramas (876 distinct IMDb title IDs — a few titles share names) airing between January 1990 and October 2018. Every column is fully populated: there are zero missing values for titleId, seasonNumber, title, date, av_rating, share, or genres. The sole numeric outcome is av_rating (the IMDb-weighted season average) which ranges from 2.704 to 9.682 with a mean of 8.06 and a median of 8.12. Already from this profile we see TV-drama ratings on IMDb skew strongly upward — this is normal for IMDb, which is a self-selected audience that mostly votes on shows it likes.

raw_evidence.label: The 'Golden Age of Television' thesis
raw_evidence.content: The cultural shorthand 'Golden Age of Television' usually refers to a renaissance of dramatic television that critics date to January 1999 — the premiere of HBO's The Sopranos. Across the 2000s, anti-hero-driven prestige dramas (The Wire, Mad Men, Breaking Bad) raised the formal ambition of the medium until production values began to rival cinema. By the mid-2010s the same trend had broadened into 'Peak TV', a phrase coined by FX chief John Landgraf in 2015 to describe a glut of scripted series. The number of scripted originals on US television grew from 210 in 2009 to 495 in 2018, the year The Economist's article appeared. The dataset under analysis covers exactly this 1990–2018 arc, which makes it ideal for testing whether perceived improvement is reflected in viewer ratings.

raw_evidence.label: Yearly mean rating drifts upward
raw_evidence.content: Mean season rating per year drifts upward over the 29-year span: the 1990–1999 decade averages 7.83, the 2000s 8.02, and the 2010–2018 stretch 8.11 — a gain of about 0.28 of a rating point from the first decade to the last. The rise is not monotonic; the late 1990s actually look slightly worse than 1990 itself, with a low of 7.63 in 1996. The break-point is 2001, when the mean jumps to 8.06 and never falls back below 8.0 again (with the mild exception of 2007). This 0.28-point gap is small relative to the within-year noise (std of mean is roughly 0.05) but it is consistent across two-thirds of the series and therefore meaningful.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_03 ===")
yearly = df.groupby("year").agg(
    n_seasons=("av_rating", "size"),
    mean_rating=("av_rating", "mean"),
    median_rating=("av_rating", "median"),
).reset_index()
yearly["mean_rating"]   = yearly["mean_rating"].round(3)
yearly["median_rating"] = yearly["median_rating"].round(3)
print(yearly.to_string(index=False))

early = df[df["year"].between(1990, 1999)]["av_rating"].mean()
mid   = df[df["year"].between(2000, 2009)]["av_rating"].mean()
late  = df[df["year"].between(2010, 2018)]["av_rating"].mean()
print(f"\nDecade means:")
print(f"  1990–1999: {early:.3f} (n={int((df['year'].between(1990,1999)).sum())})")
print(f"  2000–2009: {mid:.3f} (n={int((df['year'].between(2000,2009)).sum())})")
print(f"  2010–2018: {late:.3f} (n={int((df['year'].between(2010,2018)).sum())})")

raw_evidence.label: Hook — the flat-mean trap
raw_evidence.editorial_notes: Open by stating the small mean gain (7.94 → 8.08) so the reader sees the contrarian setup before the payoff. Numbers must be exact.

raw_evidence.label: Why a general reader should care
raw_evidence.content: TV is now the cultural form most Americans consume the most of, by hours. Whether the medium is genuinely 'better' than it used to be is a debate that animates cultural critics, network executives, and dinner-table arguments. The Economist's chart matters because it offered a rare data-grounded answer at a moment when subjective opinion ruled the conversation. It is also a useful natural experiment for anyone who wants to ask whether ratings inflation, audience self-selection, or genuine quality improvement explains the curve — and the dataset has all three signals (vote shares, genre, time) needed to interrogate that.

raw_evidence.label: Prestige-tier (>=9.0) seasons per year
raw_evidence.content: If you isolate the prestige tier — seasons rated 9.0 or higher — the picture is much sharper than the headline mean suggests. Throughout the 2000s there are essentially zero such seasons most years (1999, 2000, 2001, 2002, 2003 each have one or none). Then in 2014 the count jumps to 13, followed by 14 in 2015, 12 in 2016, and a dataset peak of 16 in 2017. By percentage of seasons that year, 1992 and 1996 had 0% above 9.0, while 2014 had 7.83% and 2017 had 6.96%. So while the mean rating drift from the 1990s to the 2010s is modest, the rate at which prestige-tier seasons are produced rose roughly tenfold.
raw_evidence.code:
df["prestige"] = df["av_rating"] >= 9.0
prestige = df.groupby("year").agg(
    n_seasons=("av_rating", "size"),
    n_prestige=("prestige", "sum"),
).reset_index()
prestige["pct_prestige"] = (prestige["n_prestige"] / prestige["n_seasons"] * 100).round(2)
print(prestige.to_string(index=False))

# Also count in the >=8.5 "very-good" band
df["very_good"] = df["av_rating"] >= 8.5
vg = df.groupby("year").agg(
    n_seasons=("av_rating", "size"),
    n_very_good=("very_good", "sum"),
).reset_index()
vg["pct_very_good"] = (vg["n_very_good"] / vg["n_seasons"] * 100).round(2)
print("\n--- >=8.5 band ---")
print(vg.to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: The 'Golden Age of Television' thesis
raw_evidence.content: The cultural shorthand 'Golden Age of Television' usually refers to a renaissance of dramatic television that critics date to January 1999 — the premiere of HBO's The Sopranos. Across the 2000s, anti-hero-driven prestige dramas (The Wire, Mad Men, Breaking Bad) raised the formal ambition of the medium until production values began to rival cinema. By the mid-2010s the same trend had broadened into 'Peak TV', a phrase coined by FX chief John Landgraf in 2015 to describe a glut of scripted series. The number of scripted originals on US television grew from 210 in 2009 to 495 in 2018, the year The Economist's article appeared. The dataset under analysis covers exactly this 1990–2018 arc, which makes it ideal for testing whether perceived improvement is reflected in viewer ratings.

raw_evidence.content: Any analysis that finds an upward drift in IMDb ratings from the early 2000s onward will land squarely on the HBO/cable/streaming pivot. The Sopranos (1999), The Wire (2002), Six Feet Under (2001), and later Game of Thrones (2011) and Breaking Bad (2008, AMC) bent the format of serialized drama. Even in 2018, Six Feet Under's series-finale episode 'Everyone's Waiting' regularly tops 'best TV episode' lists, and until 2025 Breaking Bad's 'Ozymandias' was the only TV episode on IMDb with a perfect 10.0. These are the data points the eye is drawn to in any season-level scatter — the cluster of 9.0+ ratings that appears after 2000 and grows denser through the 2010s.

The bottom of the distribution is thin — fewer than 30 seasons sit below 6.5, and the absolute floor is a single Reality-TV-tagged season at 2.70. This shape — a tall hump at 8.0 with a long thin upper tail — is what makes a 'prestige tier' visible at all.

raw_evidence.label: The 'Golden Age of Television' thesis
raw_evidence.content: The cultural shorthand 'Golden Age of Television' usually refers to a renaissance of dramatic television that critics date to January 1999 — the premiere of HBO's The Sopranos. Across the 2000s, anti-hero-driven prestige dramas (The Wire, Mad Men, Breaking Bad) raised the formal ambition of the medium until production values began to rival cinema. By the mid-2010s the same trend had broadened into 'Peak TV', a phrase coined by FX chief John Landgraf in 2015 to describe a glut of scripted series. The number of scripted originals on US television grew from 210 in 2009 to 495 in 2018, the year The Economist's article appeared. The dataset under analysis covers exactly this 1990–2018 arc, which makes it ideal for testing whether perceived improvement is reflected in viewer ratings.

print("\n=== ana_11 ===")
ex["era"] = pd.cut(
    ex["year"],
    bins=[1989, 1999, 2009, 2018],
    labels=["1990–1999", "2000–2009", "2010–2018"],
)
era_g = (
    ex.groupby(["genre", "era"], observed=True)["av_rating"]
    .agg(["size", "mean"])
    .reset_index()
)
era_g["mean"] = era_g["mean"].round(3)
# pivot for readability
piv_mean = era_g.pivot(index="genre", columns="era", values="mean")
piv_size = era_g.pivot(index="genre", columns="era", values="size").fillna(0).astype(int)
# only keep genres with at least 30 seasons total
keep = piv_size.sum(axis=1) >= 30
piv_mean = piv_mean.loc[keep]
piv_size = piv_size.loc[keep]
piv_mean["delta_90s_to_10s"] = (piv_mean["2010–2018"] - piv_mean["1990–1999"]).round(3)
combined = pd.concat(
    [piv_mean, piv_size.add_suffix(" (n)")], axis=1
).sort_values("delta_90s_to_10s", ascending=False)
print(combined.to_string())

Source: Weighted Average Ratings — IMDb Help (https://help.imdb.com/article/imdb/track-movies-tv/weighted-average-ratings/GWT2) Facts: IMDb publishes weighted vote averages, not raw arithmetic means; Some users' votes carry more weight than others | det_06: Survivorship and selection caveats. Source: IMDb — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMDb) Facts: IMDb's user base skews male and Western; Voting volume has grown sharply over time as the site grew

raw_evidence.label: How IMDb ratings are computed
raw_evidence.content: The 'av_rating' column is not a simple arithmetic mean. IMDb publishes a weighted vote average: each individual rating is reweighted by an undisclosed algorithm that down-weights suspected manipulation and up-weights long-standing, frequent voters. IMDb refuses to disclose the exact formula precisely so that vote brigades can't game it. This matters for any blog claim: when we say 'Breaking Bad season 5 scored 9.7' we are reporting IMDb's weighted average of that season's episode ratings, not a raw user mean. The 'share' column in the CSV gives each season's portion of the title's total votes, which is an indirect proxy for relative audience engagement across seasons. Because the algorithm is opaque and updates several times per day, exact reproductions to two decimal places will drift; the dataset is a 2018-vintage snapshot.

raw_evidence.label: Survivorship and selection caveats
raw_evidence.content: Three biases must be acknowledged before reading any trend out of this dataset. First, survivorship: shows that aired and were forgotten still appear, but only seasons that exist on IMDb at all make it in — very obscure pre-1995 dramas may be undercounted. Second, audience self-selection: IMDb voters skew young, male, online, and engaged; their tastes are not 'the median viewer'. Third, vote concentration: more recent shows have many more votes than older ones, so the weighted-average machinery is doing more smoothing on a 2017 season than on a 1992 season. Any rising-trend claim should therefore be hedged: it is a rise in IMDb-voter consensus, which is correlated with — but not identical to — a rise in 'objective' television quality.

raw_evidence.content: The full distribution of season-level IMDb scores is heavily right-skewed toward 7.5–8.5. Out of 2,266 seasons, 1,391 (61%) fall in the [7.5, 8.5) range. This shape — a tall hump at 8.0 with a long thin upper tail — is what makes a 'prestige tier' visible at all.

raw_evidence.label: Why a general reader should care
raw_evidence.content: TV is now the cultural form most Americans consume the most of, by hours. Whether the medium is genuinely 'better' than it used to be is a debate that animates cultural critics, network executives, and dinner-table arguments. The Economist's chart matters because it offered a rare data-grounded answer at a moment when subjective opinion ruled the conversation. It is also a useful natural experiment for anyone who wants to ask whether ratings inflation, audience self-selection, or genuine quality improvement explains the curve — and the dataset has all three signals (vote shares, genre, time) needed to interrogate that.

sources.title: Peak TV Is Over. Welcome to the Era of Streaming Redundancy — TIME
facts: Scripted-original output continued climbing past 2018, peaking around 600 series before contracting

raw_evidence.label: Suggested analyses for the Analyst
raw_evidence.content: Given the dataset's columns, the following lines of analysis are most likely to produce a defensible 'golden age' narrative: (1) yearly mean and median season rating from 1990 to 2018, with a count of seasons each year as context; (2) the count of seasons rated 9.0+ per year, since that threshold isolates the prestige-tier; (3) a genre breakdown — Drama, Crime, Sci-Fi, Mystery, etc. — to see whether the rise is broad or driven by one bucket; (4) the top 20 highest-rated seasons in the entire dataset, because those are the recognisable show titles a reader will care about; and (5) for each top show, the within-show season-by-season trajectory. Watch out for: thin sample sizes in the early 1990s, and shows that span the boundary (e.g. Frasier began in 1993 but its strongest seasons aired later).

The Economist's chart matters because it offered a rare data-grounded answer at a moment when subjective opinion ruled the conversation. It is also a useful natural experiment for anyone who wants to ask whether ratings inflation, audience self-selection, or genuine quality improvement explains the curve — and the dataset has all three signals (vote shares, genre, time) needed to interrogate that.

sources.title: Peak TV Is Over. Welcome to the Era of Streaming Redundancy — TIME
facts: Scripted-original output continued climbing past 2018, peaking around 600 series before contracting

raw_evidence.label: Suggested analyses for the Analyst
raw_evidence.content: Given the dataset's columns, the following lines of analysis are most likely to produce a defensible 'golden age' narrative: (1) yearly mean and median season rating from 1990 to 2018, with a count of seasons each year as context; (2) the count of seasons rated 9.0+ per year, since that threshold isolates the prestige-tier; (3) a genre breakdown — Drama, Crime, Sci-Fi, Mystery, etc. — to see whether the rise is broad or driven by one bucket; (4) the top 20 highest-rated seasons in the entire dataset, because those are the recognisable show titles a reader will care about; and (5) for each top show, the within-show season-by-season trajectory. Watch out for: thin sample sizes in the early 1990s, and shows that span the boundary (e.g. Frasier began in 1993 but its strongest seasons aired later).

Each row is one season of one show

raw_evidence.label: External benchmark: what others found in the same data
raw_evidence.content: Independent re-analyses by the Stat Significant blog and others, working with the same IMDb backbone but extending past 2018, report a sustained rise in series acclaim that begins in the early 2000s on the heels of The Sopranos and continues through the 2010s — with a flattening or mild decline emerging only around 2022-2023, after our dataset ends. So whatever upward drift we find in 1990-2018 is consistent with a longer-running and externally-validated trend, not a quirk of one paper's methodology.

sources.title: Is TV's Golden Age (Officially) Over? — Stat Significant
facts: Independent IMDb-based analysis confirms a sustained rise in series ratings beginning in the early 2000s

raw_evidence.label: Caveats that survive the headline
raw_evidence.editorial_notes: Close with caveat and reframe: not 'rising tide', but 'denser top'. End on the fact that the headline survives the caveats — through 2018.
